record.paper_title: QCD, from its inception to its stubbornly unsolved problems
record.original_question: Can quantum chromodynamics derive Bloom-Gilman duality from first principles, where Bloom-Gilman duality is the observation that at low Q^2 a structure function shows prominent nucleon resonances that average to the scaling function measured at some higher Q_0^2 and then slide down its slope as Q^2 increases, rather than only explaining a QCD-improved realization of that behavior?

evidence.quote: Is Bloom-Gilman duality47, 48 a prediction of QCD? In spite of recent efforts,49 it is not (yet). That would require a complete understanding of bound-state production.

BGD is the observation47, 48 that at low Q2 a structure function shows prominent nucleon resonances, which “average” to the “scaling” function measured at some higher Q2 0 , and snuggly slide down its slope as Q2 increases.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. In deep inelastic lepton–nucleon scattering, let $F(x,Q^2)$ denote a nucleon structure function depending on the Bjorken variable $x$ and the squared momentum transfer $Q^2$. At large $Q^2 \ge Q_0^2$, $F$ is well described by a smooth scaling curve $F_{\rm scaling}(x,Q^2)$ predicted by perturbative QCD with logarithmic ($Q^2$-dependent) evolution. At low $Q^2$, the same structure function (plotted, for example, versus the Nachtmann variable or as a function of the final hadronic mass $W$) exhibits prominent nucleon resonance peaks.

Bloom–Gilman duality is the empirical statement that:
(i) when averaged over a suitable interval in $W$ (or equivalently in $x$), the low-$Q^2$ resonance structure of $F(x,Q^2)$ reproduces the high-$Q^2$ scaling curve $F_{\rm scaling}(x,Q_0^2)$; and
(ii) as $Q^2$ increases, the locally averaged resonance curve smoothly slides down along the scaling curve, matching its slope, until the resonances dissolve into the scaling regime.

Problem. Starting from the QCD Lagrangian (quarks and gluons with the standard non-Abelian gauge interaction) alone, derive Bloom–Gilman duality from first principles. That is, prove rigorously, without postulating a hadronic spectrum or invoking phenomenological models of bound-state production, that the exact electromagnetic structure function of the nucleon defined by QCD necessarily exhibits the resonance/scaling matching and sliding behavior described in (i)–(ii).
artifact.status_search_result: A first-principles QCD derivation of Bloom–Gilman duality remains an open problem. Recent work (e.g., light-front holographic QCD analyses from 2021) frames it as the "mystery of Bloom–Gilman duality" and provides partial/model-based insights, while reviews state the origin lies in confinement physics not yet derived from QCD. Operator product expansion approaches reformulate but do not explain the phenomenon from first principles.

status_evidence.title: The Mystery of Bloom-Gilman Duality: A Light Front Holographic QCD Perspective
status_evidence.snippet: The underlying origin of the duality phenomenon in deep inelastic scattering is deeply buried within the confinement aspects of QCD, and its origin remains a mystery.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2021, deriving Bloom–Gilman duality from QCD first principles is still considered an unsolved problem.

status_evidence.title: Quark–hadron duality in electron scattering
status_evidence.snippet: OPE/twist reformulation classifies duality-violating terms but falls short of explaining why multi-parton correlations are suppressed and how resonance physics gives way to scaling.
status_evidence.claim: Existing QCD-based reformulations do not constitute a first-principles derivation of duality.
